name: Snaffler - Credential and Sensitive File Discovery
description: Automated sensitive file hunter — enumerates all accessible shares across a domain and searches file contents/names for credentials, keys, config files, and other sensitive data. Runs from a Windows domain-joined host. Snaffler uses a classifier system to prioritize high-confidence finds (passwords, private keys, connection strings).
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHAT SNAFFLER FINDS ===
Snaffler uses a tiered classifier system (Red/Yellow/Green/Black) to rank findings:
  Red   → highest confidence: private keys (.pem, .key), KeePass databases (.kdbx),
           wallet files, password manager exports, .rdp files with passwords
  Yellow → high confidence: .config files with connection strings, web.config,
           appsettings.json with DB creds, .ini files with passwords,
           PowerShell scripts with hardcoded creds, .bat files with net commands
  Green  → medium: .xml files, .txt files with 'password' in content,
           .ps1 files, deployment scripts
  Black  → noise, excluded by default

=== KEY FLAGS ===
  -s          → share enumeration (enumerate all domain shares first)
  -d <domain> → target domain (e.g., INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL)
  -o <file>   → output log file
  -v data     → verbosity: show file content matches (not just filenames)
  -i <ip>     → target specific host instead of full domain
  -c          → specify a specific share path

=== OUTPUT FORMAT ===
Snaffler.log entries:
  [yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss] [Red] {GP} \\SERVER\Share\path\to\file.kdbx
  [yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss] [Yellow] {CS} \\SERVER\Share\web.config - password=SQL_p@ssw0rd!

Focus on Red first, then Yellow. Parse with:
  Select-String -Path snaffler.log -Pattern 'password|cred|secret|key' -CaseSensitive:$false

=== WHY SNAFFLER IN THE KILL CHAIN ===
After gaining initial domain access, Snaffler is often faster than manual share
enumeration for finding:
  - Database connection strings (SQL creds → lateral movement)
  - SSH/RDP private keys (direct access to Linux/Windows systems)
  - Service account credentials in deployment scripts
  - KeePass databases (crack with hashcat mode 13400)
  - Jenkins/CI config files with stored credentials

=== OPSEC ===
Loud — touches every accessible share across the domain via SMB.
Generates significant network traffic and share access logs.
Run during business hours to blend with legitimate file access.
Use -i to scope to specific servers rather than domain-wide sweep.

defense.why_it_works: Snaffler crawls accessible domain shares hunting files likely to contain secrets (configs, keys, backups) using keyword/extension rules.
defense.prerequisites: Domain-user access and reachable file shares.
defense.impact: A prioritised list of secret-bearing files across the domain's shares.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1135/T1552.001] one host enumerating many shares and opening many files (SMB access spikes / 5145); Snaffler's fan-out pattern.
defense.artifacts: Mass SMB share/file access from one host; the results log.
defense.prevention: Least-privilege share ACLs; share-access auditing; alert on one-to-many share crawling; honeytoken files.
defense.evasion: Throttle and scope the crawl to fewer shares to reduce the fan-out signature.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects
